## The shape of the bug (it has recurred four times)

`getNextWorkItem` is a three-tier ladder. Tiers 1–2 query
`harness_shared.harness_features_consolidated` (the FEATURE family). **Tier 3 is the only
tier that can serve issue-family work** — bug/change/task, via `claimNextIssueWorkItem` over
`harness_shared.work_items`.

That asymmetry is what makes tier 3 a starvation trap. Break tier 3 and a fleet whose entire
lane is bugs claims *nothing*, while every diagnostic still reports a healthy lane — because
the read path (`work_items:claimable`, `aggregateIssueClaimExclusions`) and the write-time
`set_claim_spec` preview are different code. The failure is silent and inverted: **the more
carefully a leader scopes the spec, the emptier the lane gets.**

Four incidents, same tier: EI-10062 (id-allowlist leaked) → WI-4309 (fix over-corrected,
skipped tier 3 entirely) → WI-5275 (an id leaf under `any` starved a whole fleet) →
EI-18665895916759270 (below).

## The specific trap: not every leg may be compiled into the issue query

EI-18665895916759270's first half was real and the fix was right: tier 3 used to receive only
`{issueKinds, ids, excludeIds}`, so a `not:{title glob '*p2p*'}` leg was **invisible** to the
claim SQL. Tier 3 drew a violator, and the post-claim `matchesWorkItemClaimSpec` re-check
released it and retried — inside `MAX_PLAN_LANE_ATTEMPTS` (5). On a narrow lane (measured:
2.4% of the lane matched the spec) five draws essentially never land a match, so `get_next`
reported a **false drain on ~88% of pulls**, at 30–40s per miss (five claim+release
round-trips) while `work_items:claimable` correctly reported 43 claimable.

The fix — compile the spec's filter and hand it to the claim query, unifying the CLAIM path
with the READ path — is correct. But compiling the **raw** tree re-broke the tier a different
way:

```ts
// WRONG: carries `kind = 'feature'` into a query whose rows are ALL bug/change/task
const specFilterSql = compileFilter(sql, spec.view.filter);
```

Every row in `harness_shared.work_items` is bug/change/task, so a `kind = 'feature'` leaf is
**unsatisfiable** there. The compiled predicate is effectively `FALSE`, tier 3 matches zero
rows, and WI-1407's "feature family dry ⇒ fall through to an adjacent open issue" contract
silently dies.

> Worth noting how it presented: the only visible symptom was one red integration test
> (`get-next.integration.test.ts`, tier 3), filed twice as a *test* problem (WI-5836,
> EI-18667781399356821) rather than as the delivery-blocking scheduler regression it was.
> That red gate was itself what kept the first-half fix from ever deploying.

## The rule

Tier 3's whole purpose is to **widen past the feature-family `kind` constraint**. So:

| leg | compile it into the issue query? |
|---|---|
| `kind = 'feature'` / `kind in ['feature','chunk']` (no issue kind) | **No** — strip it. That is the constraint the tier exists to widen past. |
| `kind in ['bug','change']`, `kind != 'feature'`, a `kind` glob | **Yes** — a genuine lane constraint; compiling it is the narrowing you want. |
| everything else — `title`, `paths`, `plan`, `tags`, `not`, `any` | **Yes** — this is the half that was missing and caused the false drains. |

`stripFeatureOnlyKindLeaves()` implements exactly that, at the same conservative shapes as its
sibling `widenPastKind` (a bare leaf, or one directly inside a top-level `all`). A `kind` leaf
nested under `any`/`not` is left compiled — dropping it would change OR/NOT semantics, and
leaving it can only ever narrow, never over-serve.

### Do not delegate the issue-kind narrowing to `issueKindsForFallback`

Tempting, since it already extracts an issue-kind lane constraint. Don't: its `walk()` returns
`false` — i.e. gives up and yields `undefined`, meaning *unrestricted* — the moment it meets an
`any` or `not` **anywhere** in the tree. So for a perfectly ordinary spec like

```
all[ { kind in ['bug'] }, any[ … ] ]
```

it reports no lane constraint at all, and a bug-only fleet becomes free to claim a reserved
`task`. Compiling the issue-kind leaf into SQL is strictly safer.

## If you touch tier 3, assume you have broken it

The tier's failure mode is silent (a plausible-looking "nothing claimable"), and the post-claim
re-check will *mask* an over-broad narrowing while quietly destroying throughput. Run
`lib/scheduler/get-next.integration.test.ts` — its `tier 3:` block encodes all four incidents
above — and verify your change **fails** it when reverted, not merely that it passes.

Related: `work_items:claimable` is the read-side oracle; if it and `get_next` disagree about a
spec, that disagreement is itself the bug (they share `compileFilter` precisely so they can't).
